Marketing.q: A bakery owner says, "We don't do marketing; we just bake." But she surveys customers, adds a gluten-free line they asked for, and posts specials online. What's the best response?
Marketing.right: She is marketing: all of that counts
wrong: She's right, because marketing only means paying for advertisements on TV or online
Marketing is far bigger than ads.
Surveys and new products are marketing too.
Marketing.exp: Marketing covers understanding customers, making what they want and persuading them to buy.

Marketing.q: In the circus analogy, which job is MARKETING?
wrong: The sign that says "Circus Tonight" posted on the wall outside the town hall
Marketing.exp: Marketing is the whole plan: advertising, promotion, publicity, PR and sales.

Advertising.q: A new gym puts up billboards around town reading "Grand opening Saturday." Which piece of the circus analogy is this?
wrong: Publicity, because many people in town will see the billboards on their drive
Publicity is news coverage, not your own sign.
Advertising.exp: A message announcing the product is advertising: the circus sign.

Advertising.q: Which is the clearest difference between advertising and publicity?
wrong: Advertising is always free, while publicity always costs the business a lot of money
Advertising.exp: The business writes its own ad; publicity is what the news decides to say.

Publicity.q: A local TV station runs a story about a food truck that feeds firefighters for free. The owner didn't pay for it. This is:
wrong: Media advertising, because the story was shown on television to thousands of viewers
Ads are messages the business places.

Publicity.q: Why can publicity be risky for a business?
Publicity.right: The media decides what the story says
wrong: It is the most expensive way to reach customers, so it uses up the marketing budget
Publicity.exp: The elephant in the flower bed made the news: the business doesn't control the story.

Demographics.q: A skate shop learns its buyers are mostly 14 to 22 years old and live within 5 miles. What kind of data is this?
wrong: Psychographic, because it tells the shop why these teenagers like to skateboard
Age and location are measurable traits.
Demographics.exp: Age and location are demographics: WHO buys.

Demographics.q: Which piece of customer data is demographic?
wrong: A love of outdoor adventure and caring deeply about protecting the environment

Psychographics.q: Jamba Juice learns its customers value convenience and like customizing their drinks. This is:
wrong: Demographic data, because it describes the students and young adults who buy juice
A profile is a made-up sample customer.
Psychographics.exp: Values and lifestyle preferences are psychographics.

Psychographics.q: Fiji, Liquid Death and Great Value all sell water. What mostly separates their buyers?
wrong: Their ages, because each brand only sells to one specific age group of customers
The brands differ in image: luxury, edgy, budget.
Psychographics.exp: Luxury, edgy humor and budget convenience are psychographic appeals.

Market segmentation.q: A sneaker company divides buyers into serious runners, casual walkers and fashion buyers. What is it doing?
wrong: Targeting, because it is choosing to sell to all three groups at the same time
Dividing is segmentation; choosing is targeting.
That's how the brand is seen.
Market segmentation.exp: Dividing customers into similar groups is segmentation: slicing the pie.

Market segmentation.q: Why do businesses segment their market?
wrong: To make sure every single person in the country sees exactly the same advertisement
Market segmentation.exp: Similar groups respond alike, so each can get a message that fits.

Targeting.q: After dividing its market, the sneaker company focuses its ads on serious runners. What step is this?
wrong: Segmentation, because the company is still dividing up customers into different groups
Targeting.exp: Choosing which slice to eat is targeting.

Targeting.q: What is the MAIN benefit of targeting?
wrong: It guarantees that every customer in the target group will definitely buy the product
Targeting.exp: Focusing on likely buyers cuts wasted spending and shapes branding, pricing and ads.

Target customers.q: A $300 noise-canceling headphone brand has a small ad budget. Which group is the BEST target?
Target customers.right: Frequent flyers who work while traveling
wrong: Every teenager in the country, since teenagers listen to more music than any other age group
People who rarely listen to audio
Customers who only buy the cheapest earbuds
Target customers.exp: Target customers are the buyers most likely to purchase.

Target customers.q: A brand aimed at budget shoppers starts targeting luxury buyers instead. What else would MOST likely need to change?
wrong: Nothing else, because the target customer has no effect on any other marketing decisions
Targeting shapes branding, pricing and ads.
Target customers.exp: The target shapes every other marketing choice.

Customer profile.q: Adventure Bound describes "Eco-Explorer Erika, 38, earns $160k, loves sustainable travel." Erika is:
wrong: A real customer whose information the company collected through its online rewards app
She's made up as a sample.
A market is a group, not one person.
Customer profile.exp: A customer profile is a fictional sample customer.

Customer profile.q: Why include psychographics in a customer profile and not just demographics?
Customer profile.right: To capture why the person buys
wrong: Because demographics are against the law to collect when building a customer profile
Customer profile.exp: A profile combines who (demographics) with why (psychographics).

Digital data collection.q: A clothing website records which items each shopper views and buys. This is:
wrong: Traditional data collection, because the company is learning what its shoppers want
Tracking clicks and purchases is digital.
Digital data collection.exp: Click-tracking and purchase history are digital collection.

Digital data collection.q: What is the BIGGEST advantage of tracking purchases over asking shoppers in a survey?
Digital data collection.right: It shows what people actually do
wrong: It always costs nothing and never raises any privacy concerns with customers
Behavior data shows what, not why.
Digital data collection.exp: Tracking records real behavior; surveys record what people say.

Traditional data collection.q: A restaurant hands out comment cards and interviews regulars. This is:
wrong: Digital data collection, because the restaurant will type the answers into a computer later
Traditional data collection.exp: Surveys, interviews and focus groups are traditional methods.

Traditional data collection.q: When is an interview MOST useful compared with cookies and click-tracking?
Traditional data collection.right: When you need to know why
wrong: When you need to count exactly how many people visited your website last month
When you want the cheapest data
You need to reach them to ask.
Traditional data collection.exp: Asking people directly reveals reasons that clicks don't.

Third-party data.q: A startup with no customers yet buys a list of local households with young children from a data company. This is:
wrong: Primary research, because the startup is going to use the list to find its own customers
A list isn't a sample person.
Third-party data.exp: Data bought from outside companies is third-party data.

Third-party data.q: Which is the BIGGEST risk of using third-party data?
Third-party data.right: Customers may not know their data was shared
wrong: It is always less accurate than any data that the business collects on its own
It is illegal to buy any data
Third-party data.exp: Using data customers don't know about raises privacy concerns.

Customer relationships.q: After a customer's dog died, Chewy refunded her order and sent flowers. What was Chewy MOST likely building?
wrong: A sales promotion, because the company gave the customer her money back on the order
A refund here builds loyalty, not a quick sale.

Customer relationships.q: Which tool is MOST directly aimed at building customer relationships?
wrong: A one-time billboard placed along a busy highway for the month of the grand opening
Customer relationships.exp: Rewards programs, personal service and feedback surveys build relationships.

Customer acquisition cost (CAC).q: A store spends $6,000 on ads and $2,000 on promotions and gains 200 new customers. What is its CAC?
wrong: $30, because only the $6,000 spent on ads is divided by the 200 new customers
Promotion is an acquisition cost too.

Customer acquisition cost (CAC).q: Two ads each brought 100 new customers. Ad A cost $1,500; Ad B cost $3,000. Which is better on CAC?
wrong: Ad B, because spending more money on an ad always brings in better-quality customers

Customer lifetime value (CLV).q: A coffee shop's regular spends $5 a visit, 3 times a week, for 4 years. What is she MOST valuable as?
wrong: A low-value customer, because each of her individual purchases is only five dollars
Small purchases add up over time.
Customer lifetime value (CLV).exp: Lifetime value counts what she spends over years, not one visit.

Customer lifetime value (CLV).q: Adventure Bound's loyalty program rewards repeat bookings. Which number is it MAINLY trying to raise?
wrong: Acquisition cost, because loyalty programs are mostly used to attract brand new customers
It rewards existing customers; CAC should fall.
Customer lifetime value (CLV).exp: Loyalty programs aim to raise lifetime value.

Relationship payoff.q: A gym's members start referring their friends. What happens to its CAC?
wrong: It goes up, because the gym now has many more new members to keep track of
Relationship payoff.exp: Referrals bring new customers without ad spending, lowering CAC.

Relationship payoff.q: Jamba Juice's rewards app works on both key numbers. Which pairing is correct?
wrong: Higher CAC and lower LTV, since the app's rewards cost the company money on every order
Relationship payoff.exp: Strong relationships lower acquisition cost and raise lifetime value.

Data privacy risk.q: An app shares users' location with advertisers, explained only in fine print. What's the MAIN problem?
Data privacy risk.right: Users don't understand how their data is used
wrong: Nothing, because anything written in the terms and conditions is automatically ethical
Legal fine print doesn't build trust.
Data privacy risk.exp: Privacy violations happen when customers don't know or understand how data is used.

Data privacy risk.q: Why should a business care about privacy even if no law is broken?
Data privacy risk.right: Customers who feel misled stop trusting it
wrong: Privacy only matters for very large companies that are listed on the stock market
Privacy has no effect on sales

Data breach.q: Adventure Bound stores customers' card numbers unencrypted, and hackers steal them. This is:
wrong: A privacy risk only, because the company never meant for the card numbers to be stolen
Exposed data from poor security is a breach.
Data breach.exp: Poor security that exposes data is a breach, risking fraud and identity theft.

Data breach.q: Besides fraud against customers, what is the BIGGEST cost of a breach to the business?
wrong: Its products become illegal to sell, since a breach cancels all of its business licenses

Consumer behavior.q: A store owner asks why shoppers pick up snacks at the register but walk past the same snacks in aisle 5. Which field studies this?
wrong: Quality control, because the snacks in aisle 5 might be damaged or past their dates
The question is about buying decisions.
Consumer behavior.exp: Why and how people decide to buy is consumer behavior.

Consumer behavior.q: Which question is MOST clearly a consumer-behavior question?
Consumer behavior.right: Why do customers choose our brand over a rival's?
wrong: How many units can our factory make each day if we add one more shift of workers?
Consumer behavior.exp: Consumer behavior asks why and how people buy.

Planned vs. impulse buying.q: Maya grabs a candy bar while waiting in the checkout line. This is MOST likely:
wrong: A planned purchase, because she has bought candy bars at this store many times before
Grabbed on the spot, not planned.
Planned vs. impulse buying.exp: Decisions made on the spot are impulsive.

Planned vs. impulse buying.q: A family spends three months comparing minivans before buying one. This is MOST likely:
wrong: An impulse purchase, because the family bought the minivan right after the final test drive
Planned vs. impulse buying.exp: Carefully thought-out decisions are planned purchases.

Habit buying.q: Jordan has bought the same toothpaste for 10 years without checking other brands. What does this show?
wrong: Scarcity, because Jordan worries the toothpaste might sell out before the next shopping trip
Habit buying.exp: Once buying is a habit, customers stop considering alternatives.

Habit buying.q: Why is it so hard for a new cereal brand to win customers away from established brands?
wrong: Because cereal is a necessity, so shoppers never consider switching to a brand they don't know
Habit, not necessity, is the main barrier here.
Habit buying.exp: Habits mean customers stop looking at alternatives.

Purchasing patterns.q: A grocery app notices a family orders milk, eggs and bread every Sunday night. This is:
wrong: An impulse purchase, because the family places the order late at night on the weekend
Purchasing patterns.exp: Typical habits of what, when and how often are purchasing patterns.

Purchasing patterns.q: How could the grocery app BEST use that Sunday pattern?
wrong: Raise the price of milk, eggs and bread for every customer on every single day of the week
That ignores the pattern and risks losing them.
Run a TV ad on Tuesday
Purchasing patterns.exp: Knowing when people buy lets a business reach them at the right moment.

Technology and buying.q: Before buying a TV in a store, a shopper checks prices and reviews on her phone. What does this show?
wrong: Situational factors no longer matter, because shoppers can now buy anything from home instead
Technology and buying.exp: Phones make it easy to compare prices, read reviews and buy instantly.

Technology and buying.q: How does easy online price comparison MOST likely affect a store selling identical products?
Technology and buying.right: Buyers react more to its prices
wrong: Buyers react less to its prices, because they trust the store more once they see online reviews
Easy comparing makes buyers more sensitive.
Technology and buying.exp: When comparing is easy, buyers switch more readily.

Consumer protection laws.q: A company advertises "cures colds in one hour" with no evidence. Which rules is it MOST likely breaking?
wrong: Channel restrictions, because cold medicine can only be sold through licensed pharmacies
The problem is the false claim.
Consumer protection laws.exp: Consumer protection laws guard against false advertising.

Consumer protection laws.q: Who do consumer protection laws MAINLY protect?
wrong: Businesses that are competing against much larger rivals with more money to spend
Consumer protection laws.exp: They protect buyers from fraud, false ads, unsafe products and deception.

Why study consumer behavior.q: A shoe brand studies why runners quit using its app. What is the MOST likely payoff?
wrong: It no longer needs to do any other kind of market research about its customers again
Why study consumer behavior.exp: Understanding buyers improves products, service and profit.

Why study consumer behavior.q: Which result BEST shows a business using consumer behavior insights?
Why study consumer behavior.right: Moving popular items near the entrance
wrong: Paying its suppliers on time every month so that it keeps getting good prices
Why study consumer behavior.exp: Using how people shop to shape the store is applied consumer behavior.

Personal factors.q: A retiree on a fixed income chooses store-brand products. Which factor MOST influences her?
wrong: Social, because her friends at the senior center tell her which store brands to buy
Personal factors.exp: Age and income are personal factors.

wrong: A celebrity's post that recommends a new energy drink to millions of followers
Personal factors.exp: Personal factors are traits like age, income, education and occupation.

Psychological factors.q: After a bad experience with a laptop brand, Sam refuses to buy it again. Which factor is this?
wrong: Personal, because Sam is a college student who doesn't have much money for laptops
Psychological factors.exp: Past experiences and perceptions are psychological.

Psychological factors.q: A buyer believes organic food is healthier and pays more for it. Which factor drives this?
wrong: Demographic, because people with more education are more likely to buy organic food
The scenario points to her belief.
Psychological factors.exp: Beliefs and motivations are psychological factors.

Social and cultural factors.q: A teen buys sneakers because everyone on his team wears them. Which factor is this?
wrong: Psychological, because the teen personally believes the sneakers are good for basketball
The cause given is his teammates.
Social and cultural factors.exp: Influence from friends and peers is social.

Social and cultural factors.q: A family buys certain foods every year for a holiday its culture celebrates. Which factor is this?
wrong: Situational, because the holiday is only once a year and the food is only bought around then
Social and cultural factors.exp: Culture and family traditions are social and cultural factors.

Situational factors.q: A shopper buys an umbrella at a gas station because it suddenly started pouring. Which factor is this?
wrong: Psychological, because the shopper believes that umbrellas are useful to have in the car
The trigger is the sudden rain.
Situational factors.exp: Temporary conditions like weather and location are situational.

Situational factors.right: The product being out of stock
wrong: The buyer's long-held belief that name brands are always better than store brands
Situational factors.exp: Availability at the moment is situational.

Scarcity.q: A website shows "Only 3 left in stock!" Which principle is it using?
wrong: Consensus, because the message suggests that many other shoppers have bought the product
It stresses limited supply, not others' choices.
Scarcity.exp: Limited availability raises perceived value and urgency.

Scarcity.q: Nintendo makes limited consoles at launch. Which principle does this MOST likely use?
wrong: Reciprocity, because buyers feel they owe Nintendo after waiting so long for the console

Authority.q: A toothpaste ad says "recommended by 9 out of 10 dentists." Which principle is this?
wrong: Consensus, because nine out of ten is a large share of people who agree with each other
The power comes from their expertise.

Authority.q: Which ad uses authority MOST clearly?
Authority.right: A pilot recommends a travel pillow
wrong: A pop star who has millions of fans holds up the travel pillow in a social media post
Authority.exp: A relevant expert's endorsement is authority.

Consensus.q: A restaurant app labels a dish "Most ordered this week." Which principle is this?
wrong: Scarcity, because the dish might run out if too many people order it in the same week
It points to what others chose.
Consensus.exp: People follow what others are doing.

wrong: "Developed together with a team of leading doctors at a well-known university"
Consensus.exp: Pointing to how many others bought it is consensus.

Liking.q: A brand hires a popular, relatable YouTuber to show off its headphones. Which principle is this?
wrong: Authority, because the YouTuber has a lot of followers and is famous on the platform
Liking.exp: People are swayed by those they like or relate to.

Liking.q: Why do salespeople often find something in common with a customer before pitching?
wrong: To act as an authority, since sharing a hobby proves that the salesperson is an expert

Reciprocity.q: A store gives free samples, and many tasters then buy the product. Which principle is this?
wrong: Consensus, because customers see other customers tasting the samples and then buying them
The driver is the free gift.
Reciprocity.exp: Receiving value makes people want to return the favor.

Reciprocity.q: A software company gives away a free, useful guide. Which principle does it MOST likely hope to trigger?
wrong: Scarcity, because the guide will only be available for a short period of time online
Reciprocity.exp: Giving value first makes people more likely to give back.

Consistency.q: A charity asks people to sign a small pledge, then later asks them to donate. Which principle is this?
wrong: Reciprocity, because the charity gave the people a small pledge card to sign at the event
A pledge is a commitment, not a gift.
Consistency.exp: People act in line with their past commitments.

Consistency.q: A gym says, "You set a fitness goal in January; renew today to keep it." Which principle is it using?
wrong: Scarcity, because the gym membership renewal is only available for a limited time today
It leans on the past goal.
Consistency.exp: Reminding people of past commitments is consistency.

Unity.q: An ad says, "Made by veterans, for veterans." Which principle is it using?
wrong: Liking, because most people feel positively toward veterans and admire their service
Unity.exp: Shared identity or belonging is unity.

Unity.q: Which is the BEST difference between unity and liking?
wrong: Liking only works on teenagers, while unity works on people of any age or background
Unity.exp: Liking: someone you like. Unity: someone who is 'one of us.'

Market research.q: A founder wants to open a smoothie bar because she "has a good feeling about it." What does market research add?
wrong: A guarantee that the smoothie bar will earn a profit during its very first year of business
Research reduces risk; it can't guarantee.
Market research.exp: Market research replaces gut feeling with data.

Market research.q: Starbucks used surveys, focus groups and app data, then added seasonal drinks and mobile ordering. What does this show?
wrong: Research is only useful before a business opens, never once it is already successful
Market research.exp: Research tracks changing needs and guides decisions for existing products too.

Quantitative data.q: A survey finds 62% of customers visit twice a week. What type of data is this?
wrong: Qualitative, because it describes what the customers think about visiting the store
Quantitative data.exp: Numbers on how many, how much and how often are quantitative.

Quantitative data.q: A manager wants to know how many people tried the new menu item. Which data does she need?
wrong: Qualitative, because she should ask people to describe their feelings about the menu item

Qualitative data.q: Customers say the new chair "feels cheap" and "wobbles when I lean back." What type of data is this?
wrong: Quantitative, because several different customers said the same kind of thing about the chair
Qualitative data.exp: Words that explain why are qualitative.

Qualitative data.q: Sales of a snack dropped 20%. What would qualitative research add?
wrong: The exact number of snacks that were sold in each of the company's stores every week
Qualitative data.exp: Quantitative shows what happened; qualitative explains why.

Business hypothesis.q: "At least 30% of parents will pay $120 for a wagon" is BEST described as:
wrong: A vision statement, because it describes where the company hopes to be in the long term
Business hypothesis.exp: An assumption about customers to test with data is a business hypothesis.

Business hypothesis.q: Research shows only 12% would pay. What should the business do with its hypothesis?
wrong: Ignore the results and launch anyway, because the founders are confident about the idea
Business hypothesis.exp: Research decides whether evidence supports a hypothesis.

Desirable product.q: A teleporter that moves you anywhere instantly would pass which test?
wrong: Feasible, because a large company with enough money and engineers could definitely build one
Can't make it, so can't profit.
Desirable product.exp: People would want it, but it can't be made.

Desirable product.q: Before investing, a business runs interviews and finds customers don't care about its idea. Which test did it fail?
wrong: Feasibility, because the business has not yet built a working version of its product
The finding is about wanting it.
Desirable product.exp: If customers don't want it, it isn't desirable.

Feasible product.q: A startup wants to make a phone but lacks the factories, technology and expertise. Which test does it fail?
wrong: Desirability, because people already own phones and won't want to buy another one
Lack of resources is the problem.
Feasible product.exp: Capacity, technology and time are feasibility.

Feasible product.q: Which question is a feasibility question?
Feasible product.right: Do we have the equipment to make it?
wrong: Will enough customers pay a high enough price for us to earn a profit after covering costs?
Feasible product.exp: Feasibility asks whether you can make it.

Viable product.q: A $5,000 gold pencil can be made easily, but almost no one would buy it. Which test does it fail?
wrong: Feasibility, because gold is an expensive material that is very difficult to work with
Viable product.exp: Buildable but unprofitable means not viable.

Viable product.q: A product customers love costs $40 to make, but buyers will pay only $25. What's the problem?
wrong: It isn't desirable, because customers would have to spend twenty-five dollars to buy it
Viable product.exp: A product must earn a profit to be viable.

Primary research.q: BrewScape shows two ads to Gen Z viewers and counts clicks. Which kind of research is this?
wrong: Secondary, because the ads are shown online on websites that are run by other companies
BrewScape collected the click data itself.
Primary research.exp: Collecting new data directly is primary research.

Primary research.q: Why might a business pay for primary research when secondary data exists?
wrong: Primary research is always cheaper and faster than looking at any data already collected
Primary research.exp: Primary research fits your specific question and tests your hypothesis.

Secondary research.q: BrewScape uses a commercial database to estimate the size of the canned cold-brew market. This is:
wrong: Primary research, because BrewScape is using the market size number to plan its own business
Secondary research.exp: Existing data from databases is secondary research.

Secondary research.q: What is the MAIN drawback of using a government census report?
Secondary research.right: It may not fit your exact question
wrong: It is always far more expensive than running your own survey of a thousand customers
Secondary research.exp: Secondary data is cheaper and faster but may not fit exactly.

Survey.q: A company wants opinions from 5,000 customers it can compare as numbers. Which method fits BEST?
wrong: A focus group, because a focus group lets customers explain their opinions in great depth
Survey.exp: Surveys ask a large group the same questions for quantitative data.

Survey.q: What is a survey's weakness compared with a focus group?
wrong: It can only reach a handful of people, so the results can never be compared as numbers
Survey.exp: Surveys give breadth; focus groups give depth.

Focus group.q: A company wants to know WHY a small group of loyal customers loves its product. Which method fits BEST?
wrong: A survey sent to a random sample of ten thousand people across the whole country
Breadth, not depth from loyal users.
Focus group.exp: "Why" from a small engaged group calls for a focus group.

Focus group.q: A focus group of 8 teens loved a new drink. What's the BEST caution?
Focus group.right: Eight people may not represent the market
wrong: Focus groups are always wrong, so the company should ignore the results completely
Teens can't be in focus groups
Focus group.exp: Focus groups give depth, not a representative count.

Interview.q: A furniture maker sits down with five designers to learn how they choose suppliers. Which method is this?
wrong: Observation, because the furniture maker is watching how the designers act during the meeting
Interview.exp: In-depth questions to individuals are interviews.

Interview.q: Interviews and focus groups both produce:
wrong: Quantitative data, because each person's answers can be added together into a total
Interview.exp: Both give in-depth, qualitative answers from a few people.

Experiment.q: A store moves a snack to eye level in half its stores for a month and compares sales. Which method is this?
wrong: A survey, because the store will later ask customers if they noticed the snack's new spot
It changed one thing and measured.
Experiment.exp: A controlled test measuring what people do is an experiment.

Experiment.q: Why do experiments often beat surveys for predicting sales?
wrong: They always include more people than any survey that a business could possibly run
Experiment.exp: People don't always do what they say.

Observation.q: A researcher watches which aisles shoppers walk down first, without talking to them. This is:
wrong: An interview, because the researcher will learn about the shoppers by spending time near them

Observation.q: What's the main difference between observation and an experiment?
wrong: Observation always uses a large sample, while experiments use only one or two people
Observation.exp: Experiments control a change; observations watch natural behavior.

A/B testing.q: A website shows half its visitors "Buy Now" and half "Add to Cart," then keeps the button with more sales. This is:
wrong: A focus group, because the company is learning which button its customers say they like more
A/B testing.exp: Comparing two versions with real users is an A/B test.

A/B testing.q: Netflix shows different thumbnails for the same show to different users. What is it MOST likely measuring?
wrong: Which users have the highest lifetime value so it can raise their subscription prices
A/B testing.exp: A/B tests measure authentic responses to two alternatives.

Leading question.q: Which survey question is MOST biased?
Leading question.right: "How much do you love our new flavor?"
wrong: "On a scale of one to five, how would you rate your overall satisfaction with the new flavor?"
Leading question.exp: Assuming love pushes people toward an answer.

Leading question.q: Why is a leading question a problem?
Leading question.right: The data won't reflect real opinions
wrong: It makes the survey take much longer, so fewer people will finish answering all of it
Leading question.exp: Bad data is worse than no data.

Unrepresentative sample.q: BrewScape surveys its middle-aged employees about what Gen Z wants. What's the problem?
Unrepresentative sample.right: The sample doesn't match the target
wrong: The questions were too neutral, so the employees did not give the company useful answers

Unrepresentative sample.q: A student surveys only her friends about a new school snack bar. What's the BEST fix?
Unrepresentative sample.right: Survey a random mix of students
wrong: Survey the same friends again next week to see whether their answers stay the same
Unrepresentative sample.exp: A representative sample matches the whole group.

Bar chart.q: Which chart BEST compares revenue from three different products?
wrong: A line graph, because revenue is something that companies track over many months and years

Bar chart.q: A manager wants to compare the number of customers at each of five stores. Which chart?
wrong: A pie chart, because the five stores together add up to all of the company's customers
Bar chart.exp: Comparing separate items calls for a bar chart.

Stacked bar chart.q: Which chart BEST shows quarterly sales for three products, with each quarter split by product?
wrong: A pie chart, because each quarter's sales can be divided into slices for the three products
One pie can't compare four quarters well.
Stacked bar chart.exp: Stacked bars compare items and their subcategories.

Stacked bar chart.q: What does a stacked bar show that a plain bar doesn't?
wrong: A trend over time that shows exactly when the company's sales began to rise or fall
Stacked bar chart.exp: Each bar is broken into subcategories.

Line graph.q: Which chart BEST shows sales from 2018 to 2023?
wrong: A pie chart, because the sales from each year add up to the company's total sales
Line graph.exp: Line graphs show trends over time.

Line graph.q: A line graph of a product's sales rises for 3 years, then flattens. What life-cycle stage does the flat part suggest?
wrong: Introduction, because the product's sales are no longer growing as quickly as they were
Introduction comes first, with low sales.
Line graph.exp: Flattening sales after growth signals maturity.

Pie chart.q: Which chart BEST shows each brand's share of the energy-drink market?
wrong: A line graph, because market share changes over time as new brands enter and leave
The question is the current split.
Pie chart.exp: Pie charts show parts of a whole.

Pie chart.q: A pie shows Brand X at 45% and Brand Y at 30%. What does this suggest about the market?
wrong: It's perfectly competitive, because there must be many other brands sharing the last part
Pie chart.exp: 75% held by two firms means a concentrated market.

Product (4 Ps).q: A company adds a waterproof case and longer battery to its speaker. Which P is it working on?
wrong: Promotion, because the new features will be the main point of the company's next ad campaign
Product (4 Ps).exp: Features and quality are the product decision.

Product (4 Ps).q: Which decision belongs to the Product P?
Product (4 Ps).right: Which colors and sizes to offer
wrong: Whether to sell through the company's own website or through large national retail chains
Product (4 Ps).exp: Product covers features, quality and options.

Price (4 Ps).q: A brand lowers its price from $49 to $39 to win students. Which P changed?
wrong: Promotion, because the lower price is a message that will persuade students to buy it

Price (4 Ps).q: Why can a very low price hurt a luxury brand?
Price (4 Ps).right: It changes how customers see the brand
wrong: Because lowering prices always makes the product illegal under consumer protection laws
Price (4 Ps).exp: Price affects sales, profit and perception.

Place (4 Ps).q: A snack brand starts selling in vending machines at gyms. Which P is this?
wrong: Product, because the snack will now be eaten by people who have just finished working out
Place (4 Ps).exp: Where and how customers get it is place.

Place (4 Ps).q: Which decision belongs to the Place P?
wrong: Running a 20% off coupon for all new customers who download the app this month

Promotion (4 Ps).q: A company sponsors a youth soccer league and runs Instagram ads. Which P is this?
wrong: Place, because the company's name will be shown at every soccer field across the region

Promotion (4 Ps).q: What are the two main jobs of the Promotion P?
wrong: Set the price and choose the store locations where customers will be able to buy it

Product development.q: Why do businesses test and iterate instead of launching their first idea?
Product development.right: It reduces the risk of a flop
wrong: Because the law requires every product to go through all six stages before it can be sold

Product development.q: Which is the correct order of the first three stages?
wrong: Design, ideation, validation, since a company has to draw up the product before it has ideas
Product development.exp: Ideation → validation → design → messaging → production → launch.

Ideation stage.q: A team brainstorms 50 ideas after reading customer complaints. Which stage is this?
wrong: Validation, because the ideas are based on what real customers have complained about

Ideation stage.q: Fortnite uses player data to come up with new game modes. Which stage is this?
wrong: Launch, because the new game modes will eventually be released to millions of players
Coming up with ideas comes first.
Ideation stage.exp: Using research to generate ideas is ideation.

Validation stage.q: NovaCore gives a basic solar-backpack prototype to hikers to see if they'd buy it. Which stage is this?
wrong: Design, because the company has already built a working version of the backpack to hand out
Validation stage.exp: Testing demand with an MVP is validation.

Validation stage.q: What is the MAIN question in validation?
wrong: What is the cheapest supply chain the company can use once it starts selling in large numbers?
Validation stage.exp: Validation checks demand before heavy investment.

Design stage.q: A team picks materials, builds prototypes and estimates shipping costs. Which stage is this?
wrong: Messaging, because the team is deciding which features it will talk about in advertisements
Design stage.exp: Prototypes, features and cost estimates are design.

Design stage.q: Prototype feedback shows mostly older hikers like a backpack. Which stage produced this, and what can it shape?
wrong: Launch; the final price, because older hikers have the most money to spend on new gear
Design stage.exp: Prototype feedback in design shows who buys.

Messaging stage.q: NovaCore writes, "Unlike traditional battery packs, our backpack charges itself." Which stage is this?
wrong: Production, because the company is explaining how the backpack will be made in its factory
Messaging stage.exp: Writing the value proposition and positioning is messaging.

Messaging stage.q: Which TWO things are written in the messaging stage?
wrong: The prototype and the minimum viable product, which are both tested on real customers first
Messaging stage.exp: Messaging explains who it's for and why it's better than rivals.

Production stage.q: A company orders a small first run of 2,000 units and sets up its supply chain. Which stage is this?
wrong: Launch, because the company has to make products before customers can order and receive them
Making it comes before selling it.
Production stage.exp: Choosing the process and supply chain and building it is production.

Production stage.q: Why do many businesses start production with small runs?
Production stage.right: To match output to real demand
wrong: To create scarcity on purpose, since small runs are always the best way to raise prices
Production stage.exp: Small runs avoid making too much before demand is clear.

Launch stage.q: A company starts taking orders and focuses ads on its most profitable segments. Which stage is this?
wrong: Messaging, because the company is now running advertisements aimed at its target customers
Taking orders and distributing is launch.
Launch stage.exp: Taking orders, distributing and marketing to profitable segments is launch.

Launch stage.q: After launch, sales are weak. What does product development suggest?
wrong: Stop all marketing at once, because a weak launch shows that the product can never succeed
Launch stage.exp: Development continues after launch through iteration.

Prototype.q: An engineer builds a rough model to check whether a folding hinge holds up. This is a:
wrong: Minimum viable product, because it is the simplest version of the product the company has made
It tests whether it works, not demand.
Prototype.exp: A prototype tests whether the product works.

Prototype.q: What is the MAIN purpose of a prototype?
Prototype.right: To test and improve the design
wrong: To win as many customers as possible before any of the company's competitors can react
Prototype.exp: Prototypes test whether it works and improve its design.

Prototype vs. MVP.q: Dev wants to know if parents will actually pay for his wagon. Which should he use?
wrong: A prototype, because a prototype tests whether the wagon's wheels and handle work properly
That tests the product, not demand.
Prototype vs. MVP.exp: An MVP tests the market; a prototype tests the product.

Prototype vs. MVP.q: A drone company tests whether its propeller survives a crash. Which is this?
wrong: An MVP test, because the company wants to find out whether customers will buy the drone
Prototype vs. MVP.exp: Testing whether it works is a prototype's job.

Positioning strategy.q: Liquid Death presents its water as edgy and rebellious, unlike calm, pure-looking rivals. What is this?
wrong: A pricing strategy, because Liquid Death charges more than most other brands of bottled water
It's about how customers see it versus rivals.
Positioning strategy.exp: Positioning is how a product is seen compared with competitors.

Positioning strategy.q: A new phone brand wants to be seen as the best value for students. What should guide its positioning?
Positioning strategy.right: How it compares with rival phones
wrong: Only its own production costs, because customers mainly care about how a phone is made
Positioning is about perception versus rivals.
Positioning strategy.exp: Positioning places the product in customers' minds relative to rivals.

Quality control.q: A bakery weighs every 20th loaf and checks it for defects. What is this?
wrong: Market research, because the bakery is collecting numbers about the bread that it sells
Quality control.exp: Inspections and testing during production are quality control.

Quality control.q: Why does quality control matter for marketing, not just for the factory?
wrong: It lets the company skip customer research, since good products never get complaints
Quality control.exp: Products that meet expectations build trust and loyalty.

Brand.q: Which is part of a company's brand?
wrong: Its factory equipment and the trucks that it uses to deliver products to stores
Brand.exp: A brand is a name, term, symbol, design or combination.

Brand.q: Store-brand ibuprofen works like a famous brand but costs less. What does the famous brand mainly add?
wrong: A completely different chemical formula that makes the medicine work in a new way
Brand.exp: Brands distinguish products and build loyalty.

Branding.q: Pancakes labeled "protein" also say "Not a good source of protein." What's the branding problem?
wrong: The package uses too many colors, so customers cannot easily read the product's name
Branding.exp: Effective branding aligns identity with reality.

Branding.q: A pizza chain known for cheap, average pizza remakes its recipe and relaunches its identity around quality, as Domino's did. What is this?
wrong: A price cut, because the chain is trying to bring back customers who stopped ordering from it
It changed its product and identity, not its price.
Branding.exp: Changing identity to match a remade product is a brand pivot.

Tagline.q: Nike has used "Just Do It" for decades across all its products. This is a:
wrong: Slogan, because it is a short and memorable phrase that appears on many of Nike's ads
It stands for the whole brand long-term.
A tagline can be trademarked but that's not the type.
Tagline.exp: Taglines represent the whole brand for years.

Tagline.q: A company wants one phrase to represent the whole brand for the next 20 years. It needs a:
wrong: Slogan, because a slogan can be changed whenever the company starts a new advertising campaign

Slogan.q: Coca-Cola's "Share a Coke" ran for one campaign. This is a:
wrong: Tagline, because it is a phrase that millions of customers around the world remember
Slogan.exp: Campaign phrases that can change are slogans.

Slogan.q: Which is the BEST difference between a slogan and a tagline?
Slogan.right: A slogan is for a campaign
wrong: A slogan is always protected by a patent, while a tagline is never protected by any law
A tagline is for one product
Slogan.exp: Slogans can change with campaigns; taglines represent the brand long-term.

Generic products.q: Which shopper is MOST likely to buy a generic product?
wrong: A shopper who is very loyal to one brand name and buys it no matter how high the price is
Generic products.exp: Generics serve price-sensitive buyers where brand loyalty matters less.

Generic products.q: Why can generic products charge less?
wrong: Because they are made from ingredients that are always lower quality and unsafe
Generic products.exp: Unbranded products save on brand building.

Product life cycle.q: What two things define a product's life-cycle stage?
wrong: The product's color and size, because these change as the product gets older on the market
Product life cycle.exp: Stages are based on demand and competition.

Product life cycle.q: The Model T sold from 1908 to 1927. What does this show about the life cycle?
wrong: Every product lasts exactly nineteen years before it is replaced by a newer version
Product life cycle.exp: Products move through stages; lengths vary (the RCA player lasted 85 years).

Introduction stage.q: A brand-new smart ring has low sales and few people know about it. Which stage is it in?
wrong: Decline, because its sales are low and the company is not yet earning any profit on the ring
Low sales at the start is introduction.
Introduction stage.exp: Low sales and little awareness mark introduction.

Introduction stage.q: What should marketing focus on in the introduction stage?
wrong: Cutting the price below cost so the company can clear its remaining inventory quickly
Introduction stage.exp: Customers need to know it exists.

Growth stage.q: NovaCore's sales jump and three rivals enter. Which stage is it in, and what should it do?
wrong: Decline; cut costs, because new competitors always mean the product will soon disappear
Growth stage.exp: Rapid sales plus new rivals = growth; differentiate and promote.

Growth stage.q: Which sign MOST clearly marks the growth stage?
wrong: Sales flattening as most of the people who want the product already own one
Growth stage.exp: Accelerating sales and a few new competitors mark growth.

Maturity stage.q: Fortnite's growth slowed, so it added new seasons and brand collaborations. Which stage is it in?
wrong: Decline, because the game's growth has slowed down compared with its first few years
Maturity stage.exp: Mature products defend share with innovation and differentiation.

Maturity stage.q: Which strategy fits the maturity stage BEST?
wrong: Building basic awareness, because most customers still haven't heard of the product at all
Maturity stage.exp: Maturity: protect share with loyalty, differentiation, lower prices or innovation.

Decline stage.q: DVD players' sales fall as people switch to streaming. Which stage is this?
wrong: Maturity, because DVD players have been on the market for a long time and are well known
Decline stage.exp: Falling sales as customers move to substitutes is decline.

Decline stage.q: Which option fits a product in decline?
wrong: Spend heavily on awareness ads, since nobody has heard of the product yet in the market
Decline stage.exp: In decline: cut costs, redesign or discontinue.

Price vs. cost.q: A T-shirt costs $8 to make and sells for $20. Which is the price?
wrong: $8, because that is the amount of money that changes hands when the T-shirt is produced
Price vs. cost.exp: Price is what the business charges; cost is what it spends.

Price vs. cost.q: A startup sells a gadget for $15, but each one costs $18 to make. What's the result?
wrong: It earns $3 on each one, because the startup sells the gadget to a lot of customers
Price vs. cost.exp: A price below per-unit cost brings no profit.

Pricing strategy.q: Which set of things should a business consider when choosing a pricing strategy?
wrong: Only its own costs, because the price of a product should always be exactly what it costs to make
Pricing strategy.exp: A pricing strategy depends on goals, costs, competition and target customers.

Pricing strategy.q: A business wants to win market share fast in a crowded market. Which goal-strategy pair fits?
wrong: Prestige goal; premium pricing, because high prices will attract the most customers quickly
Profit goal; loss leader on everything
Pricing strategy.exp: Different goals call for different strategies.

Value-based pricing.q: A company with a patented water filter that customers love prices it far above its cost. Which strategy?
wrong: Cost-based pricing, because the company first figured out exactly what the filter cost to make
Price is set by perceived value.
Value-based pricing.exp: Unique, valued products suit value-based pricing.

Value-based pricing.right: "What is this worth to the customer?"
wrong: "How much does it cost us to make one, and what percentage should we add on top of that?"
Value-based pricing.exp: Value-based pricing starts from perceived value.

Cost-based pricing.q: A contractor adds 20% to the cost of materials and labor for every job. Which strategy?
wrong: Value-based pricing, because homeowners place a high value on having their homes built well
The price is cost plus a set markup.
Cost-based pricing.exp: Cost plus markup is cost-based pricing.

Cost-based pricing.q: What is the BIGGEST weakness of cost-based pricing?
Cost-based pricing.right: It ignores what customers will pay
wrong: It never covers the company's costs, so every sale made with it loses money for the business
Cost-based pricing.exp: It can be too high (lose customers) or too low (miss profit).

Competitive pricing.q: Southwest lowers fares to match a rival on the same route. Which strategy?
wrong: Price gouging, because airlines change their fares often and customers can't always predict them
Competitive pricing.exp: Setting prices by rivals' prices is competitive pricing.

Competitive pricing.q: When does competitive pricing fit BEST?
wrong: A single seller of a patented product that customers cannot buy anywhere else in the market
A new market with no rivals
Competitive pricing.exp: Competitive pricing is common with many sellers of similar products.

Penetration pricing.q: A new streaming service launches at $1.99 a month, planning to raise it later. Which strategy?
wrong: Psychological pricing, because the price ends in ninety-nine cents instead of a round number
The key is starting low to win share.
Penetration pricing.exp: Low initial prices to grab share, raised later, is penetration pricing.

Penetration pricing.q: What is the MAIN risk of penetration pricing?
Penetration pricing.right: Customers may leave when prices rise
wrong: It always earns the most profit in the first year, which makes investors expect too much
Penetration pricing.exp: Low prices win share but aren't sustainable unless costs are low.

Markup.q: An item costs $12 and sells for $15. What is the markup?
wrong: 20%, because the three dollars of profit should be divided by the fifteen-dollar price

Markup.q: An item costs $24. The store adds a 25% markup. What is the selling price?
wrong: $25, because a twenty-five percent markup means adding twenty-five dollars onto the price

Profit margin.q: An item costs $40 and sells for $50. What is the profit margin?
wrong: 25%, because the ten dollars of profit is divided by the forty dollars that it cost to make

Profit margin.q: Product A costs $80, sells for $100. Product B costs $40, sells for $60. Which has the higher margin?
wrong: A, because it earns twenty dollars of profit on every unit and B earns the same dollar amount
Same dollars, but margin is a percent of price.

Subscription pricing.q: A meal-kit company charges $60 every week until you cancel. Which strategy?
wrong: Bundle pricing, because each weekly box includes several different meals in one package
The key is the recurring fee.
Subscription pricing.exp: A recurring fee is subscription pricing.

Subscription pricing.q: Why do businesses like subscription pricing?
wrong: Customers can never cancel a subscription once they have signed up for it
Subscription pricing.exp: Recurring fees bring steady revenue and raise lifetime value.

Bundle pricing.q: A fast-food chain sells a burger, fries and drink together for less than buying each separately. Which strategy?
wrong: Loss leader, because the chain is losing money on the fries in order to sell more burgers
Several items at a lower total is a bundle.
Bundle pricing.exp: Several products together at a lower total is bundling.

Bundle pricing.q: A cable company bundles internet, TV and phone. What is it MOST likely trying to do?
Bundle pricing.right: Get customers to buy more services
wrong: Lower its costs to zero, because customers who buy bundles never need any customer service
Bundle pricing.exp: Bundles encourage buying more by lowering the total.

Premium pricing.q: A watch brand sells an $8,000 watch that tells time like a $20 one. Which strategy?
wrong: Cost-based pricing, because an expensive watch takes much more money to make than a cheap one
The price signals status, not cost.
Premium pricing.exp: High prices that signal quality or exclusivity are premium pricing.

Premium pricing.q: Why might cutting the price of a premium product HURT sales?
Premium pricing.right: It weakens its image of exclusivity
wrong: Because lower prices always reduce the number of customers who are able to buy a product
Usually the opposite; here image matters.

Freemium.q: A game is free to download but charges for new characters and skins. Which strategy?
wrong: A loss leader, because the game is given away to bring players into the company's store
Free basic + paid features is freemium.
Freemium.exp: Free basic version, paid premium features.

Freemium.q: What must be true for freemium to make money?
Freemium.right: Enough free users pay for extras
wrong: Every single user must pay something, or else the company is breaking a consumer law
The free version must be bad
It must be good enough to attract users.
Freemium.exp: Revenue comes from the share who upgrade.

Psychological pricing.q: A store prices a jacket at $29.99 instead of $30. Which strategy?
wrong: Competitive pricing, because the store wants its jacket to cost less than a rival's jacket

Psychological pricing.q: Why does $9.99 often sell better than $10?
wrong: It costs the business less to make a product that is priced at nine ninety-nine
Psychological pricing.exp: The price looks lower than the next round number.

Dynamic pricing.q: Uber's fares rise when demand spikes after a concert. Which strategy?
wrong: Price gouging, because any increase in price during a busy time is against the law
Dynamic pricing.exp: Prices that change with demand or time are dynamic.

Dynamic pricing.q: A hotel charges more on holiday weekends. What is the MAIN reason?
wrong: Its costs to clean the rooms triple on holidays, so it must cover those extra expenses

Loss leader.q: Costco sells hot dogs very cheaply, even at a loss. What is it MOST likely trying to do?
Loss leader.right: Bring in shoppers who buy other items
wrong: Win the market for hot dogs, since that is where the company earns most of its money
The point is the other items.
Loss leader.exp: A loss leader draws buyers for other products.

Loss leader.q: A grocery store sells milk below cost. Which strategy, and what kind is it?
Loss leader.right: Loss leader, a form of penetration
wrong: Premium pricing, because milk is a necessity that people will buy no matter what it costs
Loss leader.exp: Your slides call loss leaders a form of penetration pricing.

Pay-what-you-want.q: A museum lets visitors pay any amount, with a $1 minimum. Which strategy?
wrong: Freemium, because some visitors will pay more to get extra features during their museum visit
Pay-what-you-want.exp: Customers choose the amount, sometimes with a minimum.

Pay-what-you-want.q: What is the BIGGEST risk of pay-what-you-want pricing?
Pay-what-you-want.right: Many people may pay very little
wrong: Every customer will choose to pay much more than the product is really worth to them

Pricing power.q: AquaPure's patented filter has no close rivals and loyal buyers. What pricing power does it have?
wrong: None, because a filter is a simple product that almost any company in the world could make
Pricing power.exp: Unique, differentiated products have more pricing power.

Pricing power.q: A rival launches an identical filter at half AquaPure's price. What happens to AquaPure's pricing power?
wrong: It rises, because customers will see AquaPure's higher price as a sign of better quality
Pricing power.exp: A cheap substitute makes demand more elastic and cuts pricing power.

Price elasticity of demand.q: When gas prices rise 20%, drivers buy only slightly less gas. What does this show about demand for gas?
wrong: It's elastic, because drivers did buy a little less gas after the price went up
Only slightly less means low responsiveness.
Price elasticity of demand.exp: Little change in buying after a price change means inelastic demand.

Price elasticity of demand.q: What does price elasticity of demand measure?
Price elasticity of demand.right: How much buying changes when price changes
wrong: How quickly a business can raise the amount that it pays its suppliers for raw materials
Price elasticity of demand.exp: Elasticity measures customer responsiveness to price.

Elastic demand.q: A store raises the price of one brand of bottled water 10%, and sales drop 40%. Demand is:
wrong: Inelastic, because people still need to drink water every single day no matter what it costs
Elastic demand.exp: A big drop in buying after a price rise is elastic.

Elastic demand.q: If demand for a product is elastic, what happens if the business raises its price?
wrong: It gains many customers, since a higher price makes customers think that the quality is better

Inelastic demand.q: Disneyland raised prices and attendance still rose. What does this suggest?
wrong: Demand is elastic, because more customers came to the park after the prices were raised
Prices were too low by law
Inelastic demand.exp: Customers barely reacting to price increases means inelastic demand.

Inelastic demand.q: Which product MOST likely has inelastic demand?
wrong: One brand of potato chips that sits on the shelf next to a dozen other brands of chips
Inelastic demand.exp: Necessities with few substitutes have inelastic demand.

Elasticity factors.q: Which change would make demand for a product MORE elastic?
wrong: The product becomes a necessity that customers depend on for their health each day
It costs a tiny share of income
Elasticity factors.exp: More substitutes means buyers can easily switch.

Elasticity factors.q: Disneyland gives local residents discounts. Why might locals be more price-sensitive?
Elasticity factors.right: They can decide on short notice and visit often
wrong: Locals have no substitutes for Disneyland, so they will always pay any price for a ticket
That would make them less sensitive.
Elasticity factors.exp: Time to decide and frequency make locals more responsive.

Price gouging.q: After a hurricane, a store triples the price of bottled water. This is MOST likely:
wrong: Dynamic pricing, because the store is simply changing its prices to match the higher demand
Price gouging.exp: Sharp increases during emergencies can be illegal gouging.

Price gouging.q: What separates price gouging from ordinary dynamic pricing?
Price gouging.right: An emergency and an extreme increase
wrong: Gouging only happens online, while dynamic pricing only happens in physical stores
Price gouging.exp: Gouging is a sharp increase during an emergency when demand spikes.

Price discrimination.q: A theater charges students less than adults for the same show. Is this legal?
Price discrimination.right: Yes; it isn't based on a protected trait
wrong: No, because charging different groups different prices for the same thing is always against the law
Not a protected trait in your notes.
Price discrimination.exp: Price discrimination is illegal only when based on protected traits.

Price discrimination.q: Which pricing practice would be illegal?
Price discrimination.right: Charging customers more because of their race
wrong: Charging adults more than children for a ticket to see the very same movie at the theater
Price discrimination.exp: Pricing based on race, nationality or sex is illegal discrimination.

Brick-and-mortar.q: A bookstore sells only in its two physical shops downtown. This is:
wrong: An online marketplace, because customers can look up the store's address on their phones
It's a retailer, but the format is brick-and-mortar.

Brick-and-mortar.q: What is the BEST reason a mattress brand opens brick-and-mortar stores?
Brick-and-mortar.right: Customers want to try it in person
wrong: Physical stores always cost less to run than a website does, so the brand saves money
Brick-and-mortar.exp: Place should match how customers want to buy.

Online marketplace.q: A small candle maker sells through Amazon. Amazon is serving as:
wrong: A brick-and-mortar store, because Amazon owns many large warehouses all around the country
Online marketplace.exp: Websites and apps where people buy are online marketplaces.

Online marketplace.q: What is the MAIN benefit for the candle maker of selling through an online marketplace?
wrong: Full control over how its candles are displayed and priced on every page of the site

Marketing channel.q: Which statement about marketing channels is correct?
Marketing channel.right: They're the last stage of the supply chain
wrong: They're the first stage of the supply chain, where raw materials are gathered from suppliers
Marketing channel.exp: Channels move finished products to customers: the final stage.

Marketing channel.q: A farm sells apples to a distributor, who sells to grocery stores, who sell to shoppers. What is this whole path?
wrong: A promotional mix, because each business in the path helps to advertise the farm's apples
It's the path to the customer.
Marketing channel.exp: The path from producer to customer is a marketing channel.

Intermediary.q: In "cereal maker → grocery store → shopper," which is the intermediary?
wrong: The cereal maker, because it is in the middle of the process between the farm and the store
Intermediary.exp: Businesses between producer and customer are intermediaries.

Intermediary.q: What does a business MOSTLY give up by using intermediaries?
Intermediary.right: Some control and money per unit
wrong: All of its customers, because intermediaries are never allowed to share any sales with producers
Intermediary.exp: Intermediaries bring reach but less control and less money per unit.

B2C.q: A hoodie brand sells on its own online store to teens. This is:
wrong: B2B, because the hoodie brand is a business and it is selling its products online
B2C.exp: Selling to individual customers is B2C.

B2C.q: Your class answer key classifies "cereal → grocery store → shoppers" as B2C. Why?
wrong: Because the grocery store is a business that buys the cereal from the cereal company first
That step is B2B, but the key goes by final customer.

B2B.q: A software company sells accounting tools to small businesses through its website. This is:
wrong: B2C, because the software company sells its products through its own website online
B2B.exp: Selling to other businesses is B2B.

B2B.q: Amazon earns most of its profit from AWS, which sells cloud services to companies. What does this show?
wrong: Amazon only sells to businesses and has stopped selling products to individual customers
B2B.exp: A firm can do both B2C and B2B; AWS is B2B.

Direct channel.q: A jewelry maker sells only through its own website. Which channel is this?
wrong: Indirect, because the jewelry is shipped to customers by a delivery company like UPS
Shipping isn't selling through a middleman.

Direct channel.q: A farm sells vegetables straight to a local restaurant. How is this classified?
wrong: B2C, indirect, because the restaurant will later serve the vegetables to its own customers
The farm sells straight to a business.
Direct channel.exp: Farm to restaurant is B2B and direct.

Indirect channel.q: Nike sells shoes through Foot Locker. Which channel is this?
wrong: Direct, because the shoes still carry the Nike name and logo when they are sold at Foot Locker
The question is the channel type.
Indirect channel.exp: Selling through a retailer is indirect.

Indirect channel.q: A school district buys desks through a distributor. How is this classified?
wrong: B2C, direct, because the desks will be used by individual students sitting in the classrooms
The buyer is a district, through a distributor.
Indirect channel.exp: Organization buyer through an intermediary = B2B, indirect.

Direct channel advantages.q: Vitality Drops sells only on its website. What is its BIGGEST advantage?
wrong: Reaching the most customers in the shortest time without spending money on its own logistics
Direct channel advantages.exp: Direct channels give control and customer data.

Direct channel advantages.q: Nike pulled out of several retailers. Which benefit was it MOST likely seeking?
Direct channel advantages.right: More control and profit per sale
wrong: Wider reach, because fewer stores would mean more customers could find its shoes everywhere
Direct costs more to set up.
Direct channel advantages.exp: Direct selling means control, no clearance discounting and keeping all the profit.

Direct channel drawbacks.q: After Nike left many retailers, brands like On and Hoka took share. What drawback does this show?
wrong: Less control over pricing, because Nike could no longer decide what its shoes would cost

Direct channel drawbacks.q: If Vitality Drops stays direct and goes national, what will it have to build itself?
wrong: A relationship with a national wholesaler that already has trucks and warehouses in every state
Direct channel drawbacks.exp: Direct channels need their own logistics, sales and service expertise.

Indirect channel advantages.q: A protein-bar startup partners with a national wholesaler. What is the MAIN benefit?
wrong: More control over the price that every store charges customers for each protein bar
Indirect channel advantages.exp: Indirect channels bring reach through partners' networks.

Indirect channel advantages.q: Which business would gain MOST from an indirect channel?
Indirect channel advantages.right: A new snack brand with no stores
wrong: A hair salon that can only serve customers who come into its building for haircuts
A luxury brand that wants total control over its image
Indirect channel advantages.exp: Indirect channels let new brands scale fast.

Indirect channel drawbacks.q: A new drink gets a bottom shelf while Gatorade takes eye-level space. Which drawback is this?
wrong: Higher setup costs, because the drink company had to build its own store to sell the product
Indirect channel drawbacks.exp: Indirect channels mean less control over display and competition for shelves.

Indirect channel drawbacks.q: A brand earns $8 per item selling direct but $5 through a retailer. Why?
wrong: The retailer is breaking the law by charging customers less than the brand's own website
Indirect channel drawbacks.exp: Intermediaries mean less money per unit.

Multichannel distribution.q: Apple sells through its own stores, its website and other retailers. This is:
wrong: A direct channel only, because Apple owns the stores and the website where people buy

Multichannel distribution.q: Why would a brand use several channels at once?
Multichannel distribution.right: To balance reach, cost and control
wrong: Because using one channel is always against the law for any business that sells nationally
Multichannel distribution.exp: Mixing channels balances reach, cost and control.

Channel restrictions.q: Vitality Drops' new formula is pharmaceutical-grade. Why must it go through licensed pharmacies?
Channel restrictions.right: A law requires it for health and safety
wrong: Pharmacies always charge the lowest prices, so selling there will win the most customers
Channel restrictions.exp: Some products must use specific channels for health and safety.

Channel restrictions.q: Some states ban buying a new Tesla in person from Tesla. What does this show?
Channel restrictions.right: Laws can limit a firm's channels
wrong: Tesla does not want to sell cars directly to customers in any state of the United States
It's the law, not Tesla's choice.
Channel restrictions.exp: State franchise laws require dealers: a legal channel limit.

License.q: A new restaurant must get permission from the city before serving food. What does it need?
wrong: A trademark, because the city must approve the name of the restaurant before it can open
License.exp: Government permission to sell under rules is a license.

License.q: Which business MOST clearly needs a license to sell its product?
wrong: A T-shirt company selling on its own website to teenagers who like music
No special license in your notes.
License.exp: Alcohol must go through licensed distributors and retailers.

Purposes of promotion.q: A brand-new fitness app's first ads explain what it does and how it works. Which purpose is this MAINLY?
wrong: Building loyalty, because the app wants customers to keep using it for many years to come
New customers need to learn first.
Purposes of promotion.exp: Promotion informs, persuades and builds loyalty; new products need informing.

Purposes of promotion.q: A coffee chain emails its regulars a thank-you reward. Which purpose is this MAINLY?
wrong: Informing, because the email tells customers about a reward that they did not know about yet

Marketing campaign.q: A shoe brand runs TV ads, influencer posts and store events, all around the launch of one new shoe. This is:
wrong: A sales funnel, because the different activities move customers toward buying the shoe
A funnel is the customer's steps.
Marketing campaign.exp: A coordinated effort around one goal is a campaign.

Marketing campaign.q: Why use several tools in one campaign?
Marketing campaign.right: To keep one message consistent everywhere
wrong: Because using only one tool is against the law for any company with a national campaign
Marketing campaign.exp: Several tools keep the message consistent across platforms.

Promotional mix.q: A $5,000 robot mower and a $2 candy bar need different promotion. What decides the mix?
Promotional mix.right: Product, target market and buying situation
wrong: Only the size of the company's budget, since bigger budgets always use exactly the same tools
Promotional mix.exp: The mix depends on product, target market and buying situation.

Promotional mix.q: DoorDash uses social ads, in-app messages, a 20% new-customer discount and community events. What is this set of tools?
wrong: Its marketing channel, because all of these activities help get food delivered to customers
Promotional mix.exp: The combination of promotion tools is the promotional mix.

Media advertising.q: A soda brand runs a Super Bowl TV ad. Which tool is this?
wrong: Public relations, because millions of people will talk about the commercial after the game
Media advertising.exp: Mass communication to many at once is media advertising.

Media advertising.q: Which product is media advertising BEST suited for?
Media advertising.right: A widely used product needing awareness
wrong: A custom $2 million machine sold to just a handful of factories after months of meetings
Media advertising.exp: Media ads build awareness for widely used products.

Social media.q: Which platform feature makes social media different from TV?
wrong: It reaches only older viewers who watch the evening news on a big television at home
Social media.exp: Social media platforms let users create, share and interact.

Social media.q: A brand's fans post videos of themselves using its product. What advantage of social media does this show?
wrong: The brand now has full control over every message that is said about its products online
Social media.exp: Users creating and sharing content spreads the brand.

Personal selling.q: SunCut gives one-on-one demos of its $5,000 solar mower at trade shows. Which tool?
wrong: Media advertising, because many people at the trade show will walk by and see the mower
Personal selling.exp: A salesperson demonstrating face to face is personal selling.

Personal selling.q: Why is personal selling usually NOT used for chewing gum?
Personal selling.right: It's too costly for a cheap routine buy
wrong: Because chewing gum is a consequential purchase that needs a lot of detailed explanation
Personal selling.exp: Personal selling fits expensive, complex purchases.

Sales pitch.q: A founder has 90 seconds to explain why investors should back her product. What is she giving?
wrong: A press release, because the founder is sharing information about her company with the public
Sales pitch.exp: A short persuasive presentation of the value proposition is a pitch.

Sales pitch.q: What should a sales pitch focus on MOST?
wrong: A complete list of every cost the company has paid since it was founded several years ago
Sales pitch.exp: A pitch presents why customers should choose the product.

Consequential purchase.q: Which is MOST clearly a consequential purchase?
Consequential purchase.right: A family buying its first car
wrong: A teenager grabbing a pack of gum at the register while waiting to pay for gas

Consequential purchase.q: SunCut's mower costs $5,000. Which promotion tool fits its buyers BEST?
wrong: A coupon in the Sunday newspaper offering fifty cents off the price of a new mower
Consequential purchase.exp: Consequential purchases need detail, demos and personal contact.

Routine purchase.q: Which tool BEST fits a routine purchase like paper towels?
wrong: Personal selling, with a salesperson visiting each home to demonstrate how to use a towel
Far too costly for a routine buy.
Routine purchase.exp: Routine purchases work with mass media or direct marketing.

Routine purchase.q: Why do routine purchases need little promotion detail?
wrong: Because routine products are always the most expensive items that a household buys each year
Routine purchase.exp: Routine buys are familiar and low-risk.

Sales promotion.q: A store runs "Buy one, get one 50% off" to clear winter coats. Which tool?
wrong: Public relations, because shoppers will feel good about the store after getting a deal on coats
The deal itself is the tool.
Sales promotion.exp: Short-term incentives to clear inventory are sales promotions.

Sales promotion.q: What is a sales promotion NOT good for?
wrong: Getting customers to make a quick decision to buy before a limited-time offer runs out
Sales promotion.exp: Sales promotions drive quick action, not lasting loyalty.

Direct marketing.q: A pet store emails customers who bought puppy food a coupon for puppy toys. Which tool is this?
wrong: Media advertising, because the email is sent to many customers on the same day by the store
Direct marketing.exp: Tools overlap: a targeted email with a coupon is both.

Direct marketing.q: What is a key advantage of direct marketing?
wrong: It reaches everyone in the country with exactly the same message at the very same time
Direct marketing.exp: Tailored messages to targeted customers can be measured.

Public relations.q: SunCut hosts a free "Green Earth" festival that the local news covers. Which tool?
wrong: Sales promotion, because the festival is free for everyone in town to attend this weekend
Public relations.exp: Community events that build goodwill are PR.

Public relations.q: Why is PR called indirect marketing?
Public relations.right: It doesn't ask customers to buy now
wrong: Because it is always handled by an intermediary such as a wholesaler or a large retailer
Public relations.exp: PR builds image and trust rather than pushing an immediate sale.

Sales funnel.q: A shopper sees an Instagram ad, reads a review, talks to a salesperson, gets an email code, then buys. What does this show?
wrong: A product life cycle, because the shopper moves through several stages before buying the item
That's about the product's sales over time.
Sales funnel.exp: The steps from first learning to buying form the sales funnel.

Sales funnel.q: Why do businesses track their sales funnel?
Sales funnel.right: To see where people drop out
wrong: To find out how much each product costs to make so that they can set a price with a markup
Sales funnel.exp: Tracking the funnel improves strategy and lowers CAC.

Digital marketing.q: SunCut moves 40% of its budget from TV to social media. What is the BIGGEST advantage?
wrong: Reaching every single household in the country at the very same moment with one message
Digital marketing.exp: Digital is targeted, personal, often cheaper and measurable.

Digital marketing.q: Why did DoorDash lean on digital marketing?
Digital marketing.right: Its customers order in the app
wrong: Because television advertising is illegal for food delivery companies in most of the states
Digital marketing.exp: Promote where the target customer already is.

Big data.q: A store analyzes millions of clicks, views and purchases to see which ads lead to sales. It's using:
wrong: A focus group, because the store is learning how its customers decide what to buy online
Millions of data points, not a discussion.
Big data.exp: Huge amounts of behavior data are big data.

Big data.q: Which question can big data answer BEST?
Big data.right: Which ad message led to the most sales
wrong: Why one loyal customer feels emotionally attached to the brand after years of shopping there
Big data.exp: Big data tracks behavior at scale.

Metric.right: Number of website visitors per day
wrong: A slogan that the company plans to use in its next television advertising campaign
Metric.exp: A metric is a measurement of performance.

Metric.q: Why do digital marketers rely so much on metrics?
Metric.right: To see what's working and adjust
wrong: Because metrics replace the need to know anything at all about customers or competitors
Metric.exp: Measuring performance lets marketers change quickly.

Impressions.q: An ad was displayed 50,000 times. What is 50,000?
wrong: Clicks, because every person who saw the ad on their screen also clicked on it to learn more
Impressions.exp: Impressions count how many times an ad is shown.

Impressions.q: An ad has 100,000 impressions but almost no clicks. What's the BEST conclusion?
Impressions.right: Many saw it, but it didn't persuade
wrong: Nobody saw the ad at all, so the company needs to spend more money to get it displayed
Impressions.exp: High impressions with low clicks means the message isn't working.

Click-through rate (CTR).q: An ad had 20,000 impressions and 400 clicks. What is the CTR?
wrong: 5%, because four hundred clicks divided by twenty thousand impressions is five percent

Click-through rate (CTR).q: Ad A: 1,000 clicks on 50,000 impressions. Ad B: 600 clicks on 20,000. Which has the higher CTR?
wrong: Ad A, because it received four hundred more clicks than Ad B did during the same month
CTR is a rate, not a count.

Conversion rate.q: A website had 5,000 visitors and 150 bought something. What is its conversion rate?
wrong: 33%, because one hundred fifty buyers out of five thousand visitors works out to one in three

Conversion rate.q: An A/B test keeps "Buy Now" over "Add to Cart." Which metric MOST likely decided it?
wrong: Impressions, because the Buy Now button was shown to many more visitors than the other one
Both were shown equally; buying decided.
Conversion rate.exp: The version with more completed actions wins: conversion rate.

Return on ad spend (ROAS).q: A $2,000 ad campaign brings in $8,000 in sales. What is the ROAS?
wrong: 6, because the eight thousand dollars minus the two thousand dollars equals six thousand dollars

Return on ad spend (ROAS).q: Campaign A: ROAS 1.5. Campaign B: ROAS 5. Which should get more budget, all else equal?
wrong: A, because a lower return on ad spend means the campaign is cheaper for the business to run
Lower ROAS means less revenue per dollar.
Return on ad spend (ROAS).exp: Higher ROAS = more revenue per ad dollar.
